title: The Heart Sutra in Japanese
hookLine: the Heart Sutra chanted fast and steady to a wooden drum in Zen halls
last: GOING FOR REFUGE, IN ONE SHARED TONGUE.

cards: In a Zen hall in Japan, a monk strikes a hollow wooden drum in a steady beat, and the whole room chants with it: kan ji zai bo sa, gyo jin han nya ha ra mi ta ji. No melody to speak of.
Fast, low, level, one syllable on each stroke. Nobody races ahead; nobody drags behind. A newcomer loses the place within a line and finds it again a few beats later, because the drum never stopped.

teach.b: First, the text. The Heart Sutra is a short Mahayana teaching from the family called the Perfection of Wisdom.

In it, Avalokiteshvara, the bodhisattva of compassion, practicing deep wisdom, sees that the five heaps that make up a person are empty, and explains this to the monk Shariputra: form is emptiness, emptiness is form.
Empty, in Mahayana teaching, doesn't mean nothing. It means nothing stands on its own; each thing leans on other things. Second, the sound.

teach.h: A CHINESE TEXT IN JAPANESE SOUNDS.
teach.b: Zen halls in Japan chant a Chinese text read aloud in Japanese sounds, so form is emptiness becomes shiki soku ze ku, ku soku ze shiki.

The closing mantra, in Sanskrit gate gate paragate parasamgate bodhi svaha, comes out as gya tei, gya tei, ha ra gya tei. Third, the drum. It's a mokugyo, a wooden fish, carved hollow and struck with a padded stick.

teach.h: THE WOODEN FISH THAT NEVER SLEEPS.
teach.b: Tradition says it's a fish because a fish never closes its eyes: a reminder to stay awake. The chant leader keeps the beat, and the room follows. Fourth, why chant it this way.
That rhythm leaves no room to admire your own voice, or to plan lunch and still keep up.

teach.h: YOU DON'T PERFORM IT. YOU JOIN IT.
teach.b: You don't perform the Heart Sutra; you join it.

teach.h: FORM IS EMPTINESS, EMPTINESS IS FORM.
teach.b: Some teachers say the meaning is for study at other times; in the hall, the steadiness is the teaching. Some Zen centers in the West chant it in Japanese, some in English, some in both.

how: In Japanese Zen temples and in some Zen centers elsewhere, the Heart Sutra is chanted together during services, in Japanese readings of the Chinese text, with a leader striking a wooden fish drum to keep an even beat.

games.q: what does “the heart sutra in japanese” mean?
o: a Japanese poem about the heart, sung slowly to a flute
a new sutra written in Japan for Zen monks to memorize
a short text on emptiness, chanted in Japanese sounds to a drum

p: sees that the heaps are empty

s: in Zen halls the Heart Sutra is sung slowly to a swinging tune
it's chanted fast, low and level, one syllable to each stroke of the drum.

so form is emptiness becomes shiki soku ze ku.

games.q: you're new in a Zen hall. the drum keeps a steady beat and you lose your place in the chant. what do you do?
o: stop and wait for the chant to end.
keep listening and step back in on the next beat.
games.why: the drum never stops, so you don't have to either. you find the beat and join again. that steadiness is the practice.

practice: Tap your knee or the table with one finger in a slow, even beat, about the pace of a calm walk, and on each tap say one syllable, quietly or in your head: gya tei, gya tei, ha ra gya tei, or simply one, two, three, four.
When you lose the words, don't stop tapping; wait for the next beat and step back in.

wordCard.voice: The Heart Sutra in Japanese. A short Mahayana teaching on emptiness, chanted in Japanese readings of Chinese characters, one syllable to each stroke of a wooden drum. Today's word.

orig.note: Sanskrit prajnaparamita, the perfection of wisdom: the family of Mahayana texts the Heart Sutra belongs to.

carryVoice: Your line: the drum keeps time. When the mind runs ahead, a steady beat can bring it back. Until next time.
